title: Given a string, sort its characters in decreasing order of how often they appear. Explain how a frequency map plus a max-heap keyed on frequency builds the result.
shortTitle: Frequency Sort (Sort Characters by Decreasing Frequency)

s1_definition.profdef: Frequency Sort is a Top K Elements problem using a max-heap. We count how often each character appears, push all distinct characters into a max-heap ordered by frequency, then repeatedly extract the most frequent character and append it to the output as many times as it occurs. This produces a string sorted by decreasing frequency in O(n plus d log d) time where d is the number of distinct characters.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a transaction reference string mixes many status codes, and a report must list codes most-frequent first. We tally each code, keep a bucket with the most frequent code on top, and pour out each code repeated by its count, starting with the one that occurred most.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count frequencies, push characters into a max-heap by frequency, then pop and repeat each character by its count.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Frequency Sort is a Top K Elements problem using a max-heap. We count how often each character appears, push all distinct characters into a max-heap ordered by frequency, then repeatedly extract the most frequent character and append it to the output as many times as it occurs. This produces a string sorted by decreasing frequency in O(n plus d log d) time where d is the number of distinct characters.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a transaction reference string mixes many status codes, and a report must list codes most-frequent first. We tally each code, keep a bucket with the most frequent code on top, and pour out each code repeated by its count, starting with the one that occurred most.

**One line to remember:** Count frequencies, push characters into a max-heap by frequency, then pop and repeat each character by its count.

sections.s2_technical:
We count characters into a frequency map with `freq.merge(c, 1, Integer::sum)`. We create a max-heap ordered by frequency, `PriorityQueue<Character> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> freq.get(b) - freq.get(a));`, and offer every distinct character. Then while the heap is non-empty we poll the most frequent character and append it to a `StringBuilder` that many times: `char c = maxHeap.poll(); for (int i = 0; i < freq.get(c); i++) sb.append(c);`.

The max-heap ordered by frequency makes each poll return the next most frequent character, so the output is naturally built in decreasing-frequency order. Using a StringBuilder avoids the quadratic cost of repeated string concatenation.

A senior nuance is that characters with equal frequency can appear in any relative order unless the problem fixes a tie-break, and if a specific tie-break is required we add it as a secondary comparator. Another nuance is that for a fixed small alphabet a counting-array approach can replace the heap for linear time. Complexity is O(n plus d log d) time and O(n) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India produces a status report from a reference string of transaction status codes, and the report must list codes most-frequent first so operations focus on the dominant statuses. This is exactly how Frequency Sort works.

Problem 2 — Sorting the raw characters alphabetically does not reflect importance by frequency. This is why we count each code and use a max-heap keyed on frequency to emit codes in decreasing frequency order.

The code defines a `StatusReportService` exposing `sortByFrequency(codes)` returning the frequency-sorted string. A `Demo` sorts a status-code string and logs the result.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: string P P F F F S P.

Step 1: Count frequencies: P appears three times, F appears three times, S appears once.

Step 2: Offer P, F, and S to the max-heap keyed on frequency. The root is whichever of P or F sorts first among the two with frequency three; say P.

Step 3: Poll P and append it three times, giving P P P. Poll F and append it three times, giving P P P F F F. Poll S and append it once.

Step 4: The final string is P P P F F F S, codes in decreasing frequency order.

```

INFO: Frequency-sorted codes = PPPFFFS
INFO: Sorted: PPPFFFS
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Frequency Sort arranges a string's characters in decreasing order of how often they appear, and it is a clean application of the Top K Elements pattern with a max-heap. I first count every character into a frequency map in one pass. Then I push all the distinct characters into a max-heap that is ordered by their frequency, so the character that appears most often sits at the root.

I then drain the heap: each time I poll the most frequent remaining character and append it to a StringBuilder exactly as many times as its count. Because the heap always surfaces the next most frequent character, the output is assembled in decreasing-frequency order without any extra sorting, and the StringBuilder keeps the appends linear rather than quadratic.

At the National Bank of India I used this to build a status report from a reference string of transaction status codes, where operations wanted the dominant statuses listed first. I counted each code and used a max-heap keyed on frequency to emit codes most-frequent first. I would note that equal-frequency characters may come out in any order unless a tie-break is specified, and that a fixed small alphabet could use a counting array for linear time, which shows an interviewer I understand both the heap approach and its alternatives.
